title: Reading Last Season's Numbers in Context
brief: How do we judge last season's stats before paying for them: games with teammates out, late-season tanking stretches, hot streaks, limited-minute samples and Finals hangovers? It must explain single-season myopia in both directions and when to sell a fill-in starter.
summary: Last season's stats are where you start, not the answer. Before the 2026-10-18 auction, check every line you plan to pay for: were teammates out, was it a tanking stretch, a hot streak, a limited-minutes sample or a Finals hangover? Then bid on the player's likely role with a healthy roster. In-season, trade away fill-in starters while their numbers are at their peak, and do so before the 2027-03-04 deadline.

sections.heading: Use last season as a base, then adjust it

paragraphs.text: Start from last season's production. Then adjust it for what has changed: new teammates, lost teammates, minutes and role. Production follows minutes, role and opportunity, and all three can change over a summer. A projection describes what can happen next. It is not a copy of last year.

Play the prediction game before every bid. Write down a realistic 9-cat line for the player: points, threes, rebounds, assists, steals, blocks, turnovers, and his FG% and FT% at his shot volume. Then ask whether that line justifies the price on your sheet. Last season's finish is not the final word, but it shows how much the player has to improve to earn his rank.

ADPs and pre-draft values tend to just follow last season's finish. If you draft straight off last year's rankings, two things happen. You miss the players you should jump to grab, and you pay early for players everyone else is right to avoid. In a 12-team auction you can bid on anyone. Use that to pay more than the room for players whose context was bad last year and less for those whose context was flattering.

The experts disagree on how much history to use. Most of the notes say to look at more than one season, for example when comparing games played, and to check a player's career range. One note pushes back: using multi-year history did not predict better than last season alone. A related split: some people say projections are pointless and you can draft from last season's rankings, and the speaker in that note disagrees. Our approach: start from last season, but use earlier seasons to check whether last year was the normal case or the odd one.

Numbers a player posts while key teammates are injured are hard to repeat once those teammates return. Scale them back. Be most careful when a player produced mainly while two or three teammates were out at once. Before you bid, check who was out during his best games and how he is used when the team is healthy.

Do not lean on stats from games when one star sat if the roster has since added other high-usage players. That data does not fit the new situation. Players whose scoring came only from injury-driven usage tend to produce much less when asked to scale back. A player's best breakout chance is the season with the most opening. When the stars return, expect a step back, not growth.

Value bench players who filled big minutes during injuries closer to their healthy-team role. One note puts that at around 150th unless something changes. Our league drafts 144 players, so 150th is roughly a waiver-level player. Pay 1 USD at most for him as a last bench spot, or leave him for waivers.

Position and lineup context matter too. A wing who piled up rebounds and blocks while playing center may lose them when he moves back to his normal position on a healthy team. Shooting efficiency also depends on who he plays with. Next to stars who draw defenders he gets more open looks than he does as the lone creator on a bench unit. FG% is a team ratio in our league, so this matters most for high-volume shooters.

Big March and April numbers from tanking teams mean little. The team is trying to lose, many players are out, and late-season usage spikes often come in meaningless games. Late numbers are inflated for two reasons: teammates sit out, and so do players on opposing teams. Discount late-season shooting in particular. Backup stats from March and April are often not real, and they stop counting once the team adds players ahead of them. One note says to be very skeptical of late-season production from Sacramento.

The notes do not all point the same way on tanking. Most say tanking-stretch stats inflate fill-in players. One note says a tanking stretch can understate a player's real value, for example when a good player's role or minutes are cut while the team loses on purpose. Another says post-deadline numbers are neither all fake nor all real. So check each case: will the conditions behind the rise or the dip still exist this season?

When you read split data, note where the split starts. One source starts second-half splits on the Monday after the trade deadline. That skips the odd stretch when traded players are moving and rosters are thin. Any big jump into top-50 numbers needs a closer look at why and how it happened before you pay for it.

When a player has an extreme hot stretch, such as a post All-Star run, use the earlier part of his season as the baseline and expect his shooting to come down. Hot shooting while teammates were injured may not last once the rotation is healthy. Look for a sample of around 45 to 50 games before you trust a shooting jump.

When many players on one team have career years at once, expect some of them to regress, often all at the same time. Fans and media tend to treat a team-wide hot streak as the new normal. Do not pay full price for every member of that team.

Watch for highlight-reel bias and narrative. Early big games can create hype that the overall production does not support. Be skeptical of preseason 'maybe he gets the minutes' stories, because opportunity and shooting spikes often do not happen. Judge the actual percentages and category output, and ask why something happened and whether it can happen again. In-season, the same rule applies both ways: do not drop proven players in a cold stretch, and do not chase hot streaks that will normalize.

sections.heading: Limited minutes, games played and Finals hangovers

paragraphs.text: Strong numbers posted in limited minutes with a lot of rest should be scaled back when you project the next season. That means no back-to-backs, or playing only every second game. Games played can also overstate a real healthy sample. One note says many of Jalen Williams' 40 games were limited-minute games while he recovered from injuries. Check the minutes in each game, not just the games count.

The reverse also holds. Playing every game adds nothing if the player's per-game production is unrosterable. Our lineups are set daily, so a player only helps on the days his per-game line beats your other options. Compare games played across more than one season before paying for durability.

Teams coming off a Finals run may have a hangover. Their players are unlikely to repeat last season's production. They often start slow, with production dips and fatigue. Defending champions tend to rest players and trim starters' minutes early in the season, and teams coming off long runs may be careful with their main players' minutes all year. Bid on these players expecting fewer minutes, not last season's full line.

sections.heading: Myopia in both directions, and when to sell a fill-in starter

paragraphs.text: Single-season myopia cuts both ways. One bad season does not make a player bad. One good season does not make him good. Do not value a player by whether he won or ruined your league last year, because last season will not repeat. Use last season's top and bottom lists as a baseline only, not as a reason to fade or buy. At the auction, bad-context seasons such as injuries, minutes limits or a tank are where you can buy below value. Good-context seasons are where you let others overpay.

Sell a fill-in starter while his numbers are at their peak. When a player who is not a real starter is putting up starter numbers, trade him then, because the numbers will not get better. Sell players whose stats come from fill-in roles before the team gets its starters back or starts trying to win, because those chances will go away. Do not wait to see the drop.

Here is how that works in our league. If you pick up a fill-in starter on waivers with FAB, hold him while the injured starter is out. Shop him to the experienced managers once there is news of the starter's return. The trade deadline is 2027-03-04, before our playoffs in weeks 19 to 21, so any fill-in starter you want to sell must be gone by then. Do not pay at the 2026-10-18 auction for last March's fill-in numbers. Bid on the healthy-team role.
